<div class="practice-actions"><button type="button" class="practice-reveal" disabled aria-controls="practice-solution-20" aria-expanded="false">Show explained answer</button><span class="practice-status" aria-live="polite"></span></div>

::: {.practice-solution #practice-solution-20 hidden="hidden"}

**Suggested answer and reasoning**

1. **Calculate census effort.** Plan X has 36 plots, measured four times, at 3 person-hours each: **36 × 4 × 3 = 432 person-hours**. Plan Y needs **24 × 4 × 3 = 288 person-hours**.
2. **Add the fixed project costs.** Travel is 120 hours, setup and training 80, and identification and data checks 70. Together that is **270 person-hours** for either plan.
3. **Compare each total with the 720-hour allowance.** Plan X uses **432 + 270 = 702 hours**, leaving **720 − 702 = 18 hours**. Plan Y uses **288 + 270 = 558 hours**, leaving **720 − 558 = 162 hours**. The correct answer is **B**.
4. **Think beyond the calculation.** Eighteen person-hours across a three-year field study leave little scope for rain delays, missed plots, replacements or necessary repeat visits. Plan Y retains the same six blocks and both slope positions, but with fewer plots per position, and leaves a much more useful reserve.
5. **Understand the trade-off.** Fewer plots may make the estimate for each block less precise. However, both plans still have only three blocks per management approach. Adding plots within blocks does not add independent management replicates.
6. **Use contingencies as part of the design.** Keep some hours unallocated for problems likely to arise. If you later add measurements, choose those that directly improve the answer to your research question, not simply those that are interesting to collect.

The arithmetic assumes that a census of every plot takes the same average effort and that the other stated costs are adequate; a real proposal would need to justify those estimates.

*Related reading:* [5.3 Replication and subsampling](05-sampling-replication.qmd#replication-subsampling-and-pseudoreplication); [7.5 Repeated censuses](07-time.qmd#following-the-same-units-and-resampling-new-units); [9.7 Non-random management comparisons](09-experiments.qmd#blocking-matching-and-quasi-experiments).

:::

:::

::::


## E. Further research situations

The additional situations use different environmental research settings. They ask you to distinguish sampling for a population estimate from sampling to understand a process, and to decide which kinds of observations address different parts of a question.


::: {.practice-exercise #practice-21 data-mode="sequence"}

<span class="practice-number">Exercise 21</span>

A researcher wants to compare daytime air temperatures in shaded and unshaded areas of several urban neighbourhoods. Small temperature sensors can be installed at 16 locations for one week. Streets with dense tree cover are mostly in older residential areas; recently developed areas tend to have less shade and wider roads.

<div class="practice-response" data-mode="sequence">
<div class="practice-step" data-mode="multi">
<p class="practice-label">Step 1. Which design decisions would help investigate whether shading contributes to temperature differences? Select all that apply.</p>
<fieldset class="practice-choices"><legend>Choose one or more options</legend>
<label class="practice-choice"><input type="checkbox" value="A" data-answer="true"><span><b>A.</b> Place sensors in shaded and unshaded locations within several neighbourhoods, where comparable locations can be found.</span></label>
<label class="practice-choice"><input type="checkbox" value="B" data-answer="true"><span><b>B.</b> Record road width, building density and other local conditions that may covary with shading.</span></label>
<label class="practice-choice"><input type="checkbox" value="C" data-answer="false"><span><b>C.</b> Put all 16 sensors in one shaded park and treat the readings as 16 independent neighbourhoods.</span></label>
<label class="practice-choice"><input type="checkbox" value="D" data-answer="true"><span><b>D.</b> Collect simultaneous measurements so daily weather changes do not become confused with differences among locations.</span></label>
</fieldset>
</div>
<div class="practice-step" data-mode="text" hidden>
<p class="practice-label">Step 2. What would this observational design allow the researcher to say about shade and temperature, and what would still make a causal interpretation difficult? Answer briefly.</p>
<label class="practice-label" for="practice-input-21">Your explanation</label><textarea id="practice-input-21" class="practice-text" rows="3" placeholder="Think about differences among locations beyond shade."></textarea>
</div>
</div>
<div class="practice-actions"><button type="button" class="practice-reveal" disabled aria-controls="practice-solution-21" aria-expanded="false">Show explained answer</button><span class="practice-status" aria-live="polite"></span></div>

::: {.practice-solution #practice-solution-21 hidden="hidden"}

**Suggested answer and reasoning**

**Step 1 — A, B and D.** Measuring shaded and unshaded places in several neighbourhoods helps avoid confusing a shade contrast with the characteristics of just one neighbourhood. Simultaneous observations also allow comparison under the same broad weather conditions. Roads and buildings may differ systematically among shaded and unshaded sites, so recording those properties helps assess alternative explanations. Sixteen sensors within one park are still observations within one park, not sixteen neighbourhoods.

**Step 2.** The observations may reveal temperature differences associated with shade under the sampled conditions. The researcher would need to consider building geometry, surface materials, airflow and local land use before attributing the entire difference to shading. A design with several comparable shaded–unshaded pairs, or a suitable intervention where possible, would offer a stronger basis for testing an effect.

*Related reading:* [5.3 Replication](05-sampling-replication.qmd#replication-subsampling-and-pseudoreplication); [9.7 Matching observational comparisons](09-experiments.qmd#blocking-matching-and-quasi-experiments).

:::

:::


::: {.practice-exercise #practice-22 data-mode="single"}

<span class="practice-number">Exercise 22</span>

A research team is investigating whether a coastal construction project is associated with changes in suspended sediment in nearby seawater. It can collect water samples from six stations on each of eight field trips. The sea is influenced by tides, winds and periodic heavy rainfall. A proposed plan samples all near-construction stations during spring tides and all distant stations during neap tides.

**Your task.** Which alternative would best distinguish location differences from variation in tidal conditions?

<div class="practice-response" data-mode="single">
<fieldset class="practice-choices" data-correct="B"><legend>Choose one answer</legend>
<label class="practice-choice"><input type="radio" name="practice-group-22" value="A"><span><b>A.</b> Keep the stations but collect more bottles from each location during its original tide.</span></label>
<label class="practice-choice"><input type="radio" name="practice-group-22" value="B"><span><b>B.</b> Sample near and distant stations during the same field trips across a range of tidal and weather conditions, with a consistent sampling procedure.</span></label>
<label class="practice-choice"><input type="radio" name="practice-group-22" value="C"><span><b>C.</b> Increase the number of distant stations, but continue to sample near stations only at spring tide and distant ones only at neap tide.</span></label>
</fieldset>
</div>
<div class="practice-actions"><button type="button" class="practice-reveal" disabled aria-controls="practice-solution-22" aria-expanded="false">Show explained answer</button><span class="practice-status" aria-live="polite"></span></div>

::: {.practice-solution #practice-solution-22 hidden="hidden"}

**Suggested answer and reasoning**

**B** makes the near–distant comparison under a common set of tidal and weather conditions. In the original plan, any difference between near and distant stations could instead reflect the spring–neap tidal contrast. Additional bottles or stations would increase observations without separating those two explanations. Near and distant stations could still differ in depth, currents or sediment sources, and before-construction or other suitable comparisons may be required to assess an effect of construction.

*Related reading:* [7.3 Timing observations](07-time.qmd#measurement-interval-frequency-and-duration); [9.4 Comparing changes](09-experiments.qmd#baci-and-the-logic-of-comparing-changes).

:::

:::


::: {.practice-exercise #practice-23 data-mode="text"}

<span class="practice-number">Exercise 23</span>

A coastal village is considering changes to its flood-warning system. Researchers want to understand how residents interpret warnings and why some households do not evacuate even when an alert is issued. They propose interviews with households selected to include people with different ages, mobility constraints, previous flood experiences and locations within the village.

**Your task.** Explain what this deliberately varied participant selection could contribute to the research question. Could the researchers use the proportion of interviewed households who do not evacuate as an estimate for the entire village? Answer in two or three sentences.

<div class="practice-response" data-mode="text">
<label class="practice-label" for="practice-input-23">Your explanation</label><textarea id="practice-input-23" class="practice-text" rows="3" placeholder="Think about understanding experiences and estimating how common they are."></textarea>
</div>
<div class="practice-actions"><button type="button" class="practice-reveal" disabled aria-controls="practice-solution-23" aria-expanded="false">Show explained answer</button><span class="practice-status" aria-live="polite"></span></div>

::: {.practice-solution #practice-solution-23 hidden="hidden"}

**Suggested answer and reasoning**

Selecting households with contrasting experiences can help the researchers understand different reasons for responding to flood warnings, including practical barriers to evacuation and differences in how warnings are interpreted. This is useful for identifying experiences and explanations that might be missed if the team interviewed only easily reached households. Because the sample deliberately over- or under-represents some groups, the fraction of interviewees reporting a particular behaviour is not automatically an estimate of the village-wide fraction. Estimating prevalence would call for a separately justified sampling approach, along with attention to nonresponse. The interviews could still inform how survey questions are designed and which explanations warrant further study.

*Related reading:* [10.8 Sampling people](10-quantitative-socioenvironmental.qmd#sampling-people-coverage-recruitment-and-nonresponse); [11.3 Selecting participants](11-qualitative-participatory.qmd#ch11-s113).

:::

:::


## Using the exercises for your final assignment

When working on your own assignment, identify the particular comparison or process you want to investigate, the observations needed, the relevant units, and how observations at those units can support the intended conclusion. Use the exercises to test your reasoning about alternative designs and practical limits. The restoration landscape, measurements and numerical costs in Section D are hypothetical and should not be copied as a field plan for your assignment.
